stem:
Nhimbe Juices is a fictional business in Gweru that makes fruit juice in cartons for shops and schools. In 2025 the owner raised the price of a carton by 10% to protect profit and cut spending on promotion by half. A rival then began selling a cheaper juice, and a supermarket chain has asked Nhimbe Juices to supply 6,000 cartons a year at US\$12.50 a carton, collected from the factory. The owner says: "Keep the price high and sell less." Labour cost does not change with output.

|  | 2024 | 2025 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Selling price per carton (US\$) | 14.00 | 15.40 |
| Cartons sold (equal to output) | 21,600 | 19,800 |
| Maximum capacity (cartons a year) | 30,000 | 30,000 |
| Employees | 36 | 36 |
| Labour cost (US\$) | 108,000 | 111,600 |
| Promotion spending (US\$) | 12,000 | 6,000 |
| Materials and other variable costs per carton (US\$) | 6.10 | 6.10 |

Capacity utilisation = output ÷ maximum capacity × 100. Labour productivity = output ÷ employees.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: From the table, state:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the selling price of a carton in 2025;
parts.explanation: The table shows US\$15.40 in 2025.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the number of cartons sold in 2024.
parts.explanation: The table shows 21,600 cartons in 2024.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate, for 2025:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: capacity utilisation, to one decimal place;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: labour productivity, in cartons per employee.
parts.explanation: 19,800 ÷ 36 = 550 cartons per employee.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the percentage change in cartons sold between 2024 and 2025, to one decimal place (give a fall as a negative number);

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: promotion spending as a percentage of sales revenue in 2025, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Analyse why the number of cartons sold fell in 2025.

points.description: The price rose by 10% from US\$14.00 to US\$15.40, which makes the juice dearer than before
A rival is selling cheaper juice, so customers have an alternative
Promotion was cut from US\$12,000 to US\$6,000, so fewer customers were reminded of the brand
Sales fell by 8.3% while revenue rose by only 0.8% (US\$302,400 to US\$304,920), so the price rise gained little
Demand appears elastic: a 10% rise in price led to an 8.3% fall in sales and the fall in volume reduced capacity utilisation to 66.0%

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The price rose by 10%, from US\$14.00 to US\$15.40, at the same time as a rival began selling cheaper juice, so customers had an alternative. Promotion was also halved, from US\$12,000 to US\$6,000, so fewer customers were reminded of the brand. Cartons sold fell by 8.3%, while revenue rose by only 0.8%, from US\$302,400 to US\$304,920, so the price rise gained little and the fall in volume lowered capacity utilisation to 66.0%.

parts.explanation: Each cause is linked to the fall in sales, supported by figures.
hints: Use the price, the rival and the promotion in your answer.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain two ways in which Nhimbe Juices could make better use of its spare capacity.

points.description: Win more orders, for example by selling to the supermarkets
Application: 10,200 cartons of capacity are unused, which is enough for the supermarket chain's order of 6,000 cartons
Promote the juice to new markets or schools
Application: more promotion could raise sales and spread the fixed labour cost over more cartons

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Nhimbe Juices could win more orders, for example by supplying the supermarkets. About 10,200 cartons of capacity are unused, which is enough for the supermarket chain's order of 6,000 cartons. It could also promote the juice to new markets such as schools, which would raise sales and spread the fixed labour cost over more cartons.

parts.explanation: Two ways, each applied to the data.
hints: Work out the spare capacity first.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Discuss the owner's view that the company should "keep the price high and sell less", and advise whether to accept the supermarket chain's offer of US\$12.50 a carton.

points.description: At US\$15.40 the contribution is US\$9.30 a carton, but sales fell by 1,800 cartons
The supermarket chain's offer gives a contribution of US\$6.40 a carton (12.50 − 6.10)
Labour cost does not change with output, so the extra contribution on 6,000 cartons is US\$38,400
Spare capacity of 10,200 cartons is enough for the 6,000 cartons
Risk: other customers may demand lower prices, or the supermarket chain may later bargain harder
Judgement with a condition, for example: accept if the order does not make existing customers demand lower prices

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: At US\$15.40 each carton earns US\$9.30, but sales fell by 1,800 cartons and 34% of capacity is unused. The supermarket chain's offer of US\$12.50 earns US\$6.40 a carton, and since labour cost does not change and there is spare capacity of 10,200 cartons, 6,000 extra cartons would add US\$38,400 to profit. The risk is that other customers will demand lower prices. The owner should accept the order, provided the supermarket chain is kept separate from the shops that pay the higher price, rather than keeping the price high and selling less.

parts.explanation: Contribution comparison and a conditional recommendation.
hints: Use the contribution on each carton and the spare capacity.

explanation: Utilisation 66.0%, productivity 550 cartons per employee, sales down 8.3%; the supermarket order adds US\$38,400 contribution using spare capacity.

stem:
Case study. Tsitsi Honey Products is a fictional family business in Chinhoyi that produces honey from 300 hives and sells it in 500 g jars. The workshop can bottle at most 10,000 jars a month and bottled 7,000 last month. Direct costs are US\$2.70 a jar (honey, jar and label) and overheads are US\$4,900 a month, shared equally between the jars. Jars are sold through three channels.

| Channel | Price received per jar (US\$) | Delivery cost per jar (US\$) | Jars a month |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Own market stall | 5.70 | 0.25 | 1,200 |
| Retail shops (direct) | 4.90 | 0.45 | 2,800 |
| Wholesaler | 4.30 | 0.00 | 3,000 |

Customers praise the taste, but 3% of jars were returned last month because lids were loose or the honey had crystallised. Each returned jar is replaced at its full cost. Tsitsi manages production, sales and accounts herself, with two helpers. A supermarket chain in Harare has offered to buy 3,000 jars a month at US\$4.10 a jar, collected from the workshop. Tsitsi worries that this would take sales from her own stall and shops, and that the workshop would be fully busy every month, with no room for mistakes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the workshop's capacity utilisation last month, to one decimal place;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the spare capacity, in jars a month.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: the full cost of a jar last month;
parts.explanation: Overheads per jar = 4,900 ÷ 7,000 = 0.70. Full cost = 2.70 + 0.70 = US\$3.40.

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: the profit on each jar sold through the wholesaler.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Use the table to:

parts.label: (i)
parts.stem: calculate the monthly income from the retail shops after delivery costs;

parts.label: (ii)
parts.stem: identify the channel with the highest income per jar after delivery costs.

options.rationale: 4.90 − 0.45 = US\$4.45 a jar, lower than the stall.

parts.explanation: Stall US\$5.45, shops US\$4.45, wholesaler US\$4.30.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the cost of the jars returned last month.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain two benefits to Tsitsi Honey Products of selling through more than one channel.

points.description: Sales are spread over several buyers, so the loss of one does not stop the business
Application: the wholesaler takes 3,000 jars, but the stall and the shops are two other sources of income
Different channels pay different prices
Application: the stall earns US\$5.45 a jar after delivery, much more than the wholesaler's US\$4.30

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Selling through several channels spreads the risk, so if the wholesaler's 3,000 jars were lost the stall and shops would still pay. Different channels also pay different prices: the stall earns US\$5.45 a jar after delivery against US\$4.30 from the wholesaler, which raises the average income.

parts.explanation: Two benefits, each applied.
hints: Use the prices and quantities in the table.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Analyse how quality assurance could reduce the number of returned jars.

points.description: Quality assurance aims to prevent faults rather than find them after production
Setting standards, such as a check that each lid is tight and a limit on storage temperature, tackles the two faults
Training the two helpers to follow the standards reduces mistakes
Fewer returns save the full cost of replacing each jar (US\$714 last month)
Better quality improves customers' loyalty and the brand's reputation

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Quality assurance aims to prevent faults instead of finding them afterwards. Tsitsi could set standards such as a check that each lid is tight and a limit on storage temperature to reduce crystallised honey, and train her two helpers to follow them. Fewer faulty jars would mean fewer returns, saving some of the US\$714 spent on replacements last month, and better quality would improve customers' loyalty and the reputation of the brand.

parts.explanation: A chain from prevention to fewer returns, lower cost and better reputation.
hints: Link each action to one of the two faults.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Evaluate whether Tsitsi Honey Products should accept the supermarket chain's offer.

points.description: The offer is for 3,000 jars, exactly the spare capacity of 3,000 jars
Contribution is (4.10 − 2.70) × 3,000 = US\$4,200 a month, because overheads are already paid
The supermarket price of US\$4.10 is above the full cost of US\$3.40, but below the US\$4.30 paid by the wholesaler and the prices in her other channels
Use of all capacity leaves no room for mistakes, and quality problems already exist
The supermarket may take sales from her stall and shops, which pay more per jar
Dependence on one large buyer is risky if it later demands a lower price
Alternative: sell fewer jars to the supermarket, or ask a higher price
Judgement with a reason
Condition or time-frame, for example: accept for a trial period while fixing quality

levels.descriptor: Balanced evaluation using the figures and the risks in the case, with a justified recommendation and a condition
Reasons for and against using some figures
General points with little use of the case

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The offer uses exactly the 3,000 jars of spare capacity and earns a contribution of (4.10 − 2.70) × 3,000 = US\$4,200 a month, because the overheads are already paid. That is a useful addition for a small business. Against this, the supermarket price is lower than the wholesaler's and her other channels, and may tempt her own shop customers to buy there instead, which would lower her income; she would also be fully busy with no room for mistakes when quality is already a problem, and she would depend on one large buyer. Tsitsi should accept for a trial of three months, keeping her stall and shops separate and fixing the lid and crystallisation problems first, and renew only if the supermarket does not demand a lower price.

parts.explanation: Contribution of US\$4,200 a month, weighed against capacity, quality and cannibalisation risks.
hints: Compare the contribution with the risks of full capacity and lost sales.

explanation: Utilisation 70.0%, spare capacity 3,000, full cost US\$3.40, wholesaler profit US\$0.90, shop income US\$12,460, returns cost US\$714; the supermarket offer adds US\$4,200 contribution.
hints: Full cost includes the overheads shared per jar.

stem: Essay. Setting the right price is one of the most important decisions in marketing.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe four methods that a business can use to set the price of its products. [10 marks]

points.description: Cost-plus: the price is the cost per unit plus a mark-up
Development: simple, but ignores demand and rivals
Competitive pricing: the price is set close to rivals' prices
Development: suits markets with many similar products but leaves little freedom
Penetration: a low price at launch to win market share
Development: suits price-sensitive buyers, but profit per unit is low at first
Skimming: a high price at launch for a new or unique product
Development: earns a large profit on early sales but attracts rivals
Psychological pricing, such as US\$4.95, or price discrimination as a further method
An example from a Zimbabwean business such as a bakery or a hardware shop

levels.descriptor: Four methods clearly described and developed, with an example
Three or four methods described with some development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: With cost-plus pricing a business adds a percentage mark-up to the cost of each unit; it is simple, as in a hardware shop that adds 30% to the price it pays, but it ignores demand and rivals. In competitive pricing the price is set close to rivals' prices, which suits a market where bread or soap products are similar, but leaves little freedom. Penetration pricing sets a low price at launch to win market share, as a new juice might do, but the profit on each unit is low at first. Skimming sets a high price for a new or unique product such as a new gadget, earning a large profit on early sales, though it may attract rivals. A business may also use psychological pricing, such as US\$4.95 instead of US\$5.00, to make a price seem lower.

parts.explanation: Four methods, each described and developed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss the factors that a manufacturer should consider when setting the price of a new product, and recommend a pricing strategy for a new product in Zimbabwe. [15 marks]

points.description: Costs: the price must cover the cost of each unit in the long run
Application: a fictional soap maker must cover materials, labour and overheads
Competition: close substitutes limit how far above rivals the price can be
Demand and customers' sensitivity to price (elasticity)
Application: if buyers are price sensitive a lower price raises sales and revenue
The firm's objectives, such as profit, market share or survival
Market conditions, such as incomes, inflation and shortages
Link with the rest of the mix: a premium brand needs a higher price
Penetration pricing builds share quickly but risks low early profit and difficulty in raising prices
Skimming earns high early profit for unique products but attracts rivals and sells fewer units
Cost-plus is simple but ignores demand
The most important factors depend on the product and market
Judgement: choose a strategy to match the product's uniqueness and buyers' price sensitivity
Recommendation with reasons, for example penetration for a new brand of soap in a crowded market
Conclusion that states a condition, such as reviewing the price after a few months

levels.descriptor: Balanced discussion of several factors with application, a justified recommendation and a conclusion
Several factors explained with some application and a recommendation

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A manufacturer must first cover costs: if a soap maker's price is below the cost of each bar, every sale loses money in the long run. Competition limits the price too, because buyers can switch to similar soaps. The most important factor for a new product is often demand: if customers are sensitive to price, a lower price raises sales and may raise revenue, but if they value a unique feature they will pay more. The firm's objective matters: a firm wanting market share will choose a lower price than one wanting quick profit. Market conditions such as incomes and inflation, and the image of the brand, also affect the price. For strategy, penetration pricing builds a customer base quickly and suits a crowded soap market, but profit is low at first and a later rise may lose customers. Skimming earns more on each unit and suits a unique product, but it attracts rivals and sells fewer units. Cost-plus is simple but ignores demand. For a new soap in a crowded Zimbabwean market where buyers compare prices, I would recommend penetration pricing, because it wins customers quickly. The firm should review the price after a few months, once the brand is known and costs are clearer.

parts.explanation: Factors, strategies and a justified recommendation.

explanation: Four pricing methods described; factors discussed and a strategy recommended with reasons.
hints: Describe each method, then develop it with an effect or an example.

stem: Essay. Productivity and quality both affect how competitive a business is.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Explain four ways in which a business can increase the productivity of its workers. [10 marks]

points.description: Training: workers learn faster and more accurate methods
Development: more output in the same time with fewer mistakes
Motivation through fair pay, recognition and involvement
Development: motivated workers put in more effort and stay longer
Better equipment and technology
Development: machines raise the output of each worker, though they cost money
Improved layout and organisation of work
Development: less time wasted moving materials and waiting
Value analysis: removing unnecessary cost from the design or process
A Zimbabwean example, such as a bakery or garment factory, and a link to unit labour cost

levels.descriptor: Four ways explained and developed, with an example
Three or four ways explained with some development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: A business can train its workers so that they use faster and more accurate methods, which gives more output in the same time with fewer mistakes. It can motivate them through fair pay, recognition and involvement, so that they work harder and stay longer. Better equipment, such as a faster dough mixer in a bakery, raises the output of each worker, though it costs money. An improved layout reduces time spent moving materials and waiting. Each way raises output per worker, so the labour cost of each unit falls if pay does not rise faster than output.

parts.explanation: Four ways, each explained and developed.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Discuss whether quality assurance is a better way of controlling quality than inspection for a Zimbabwean manufacturing business. [15 marks]

points.description: Inspection finds faults after or during production by checking products
Application: a garment factory inspects shirts before packing
Inspection protects customers from faulty goods but waste has already occurred
It adds the cost of inspectors and does not stop faults being made again
Quality assurance prevents faults by setting standards and organising every stage
It involves workers through training and teamwork (TQM, quality circles or kaizen groups)
Application: training machinists to sew correctly reduces faults at source
Fewer faults reduce waste, rework and returns
Quality assurance takes time and training to introduce, and relies on workers' commitment
A system with some inspection is still needed to check the results
For a firm with many faults, prevention gives greater savings than inspection
For a firm that makes one-off or high-risk goods, inspection of every item may be needed
Judgement: quality assurance is better in the long run, supported by some inspection
Conclusion with a condition, such as the commitment of the workers
Reference to the cost compared with the savings from fewer returns

levels.descriptor: Balanced discussion of both approaches with application, a justified judgement and a condition
Both approaches explained with some application and a judgement
Describes the approaches with little development

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Inspection finds faults by checking products, for example a garment factory that examines shirts before packing. It protects customers, but the faulty shirts have already been made, so material and labour are wasted, and inspectors add cost without stopping the faults from happening again. Quality assurance prevents faults by setting standards and organising every stage, and it involves workers through training and teams such as quality circles. If machinists are trained to sew correctly, fewer shirts are faulty, so waste, rework and returns fall. However, quality assurance takes time and training to introduce and depends on the commitment of workers, and some inspection is still needed to check the results. For a firm with many faults, prevention gives the greater savings, but for goods where one fault is dangerous or costly, every item may still be inspected. Overall, quality assurance is better in the long run for a manufacturer, supported by sample inspection, provided that workers are trained and committed and the savings from fewer returns exceed the cost.

parts.explanation: Both approaches weighed, with a judgement and a condition.

explanation: Four ways to raise productivity explained; quality assurance weighed against inspection with a justified judgement.
hints: Explain the difference between finding faults and preventing them.
